passages.original: Hodiernum hoc est, quod apud Epicurum nanctus sum; soleo enim et in aliena castra transire, non tamquam transfuga, sed tamquam explorator.
passages.english: Today's [gift] is this, which I came upon in Epicurus; for I am in the habit of crossing over even into the enemy's camp, not as a deserter, but as a scout.

passages.original: Sed ne soli mihi hodie didicerim, communicabo tecum, quae occurrerunt mihi egregie dicta circa eundem fere sensum tria; ex quibus unum haec epistula in debitum solvet, duo in antecessum accipe. Democritus ait: Unus mihi pro populo est, et populus pro uno.
passages.english: But so that I may not have learned today for myself alone, I will share with you three excellently expressed sayings that I came across, on roughly the same idea; of these, this letter will pay one as the debt owed, and the other two you may take as an advance. Democritus says: "One man is to me as a people, and a people as one man."

passages.original: An merito reprehendat in quadam epistula Epicurus eos, qui dicunt sapientem se ipso esse contentum et propter hoc amico non indigere, desideras scire. Hoc obicitur Stilboni ab Epicuro et iis quibus summum bonum visum est animus inpatiens.
passages.english: You wish to know whether Epicurus is right when, in a certain letter, he censures those who say that the wise man is content with himself and for this reason does not need a friend. This is the objection raised by Epicurus against Stilbo and against those who have held that the highest good is a mind incapable of suffering.
passages.notes: Stilbo: Stilpo of Megara.

passages.original: Nunc ad propositum revertamur. Sapiens, etiam si contentus est se, tamen habere amicum vult, si nihil aliud, ut exerceat amicitiam, ne tam magna virtus iaceat, non ad hoc, quod dicebat Epicurus in hac ipsa epistula, ut habeat, qui sibi aegro adsideat, succurrat in vincula coniecto vel inopi, sed ut habeat aliquem, cui ipse aegro adsideat, quem ipse circumventum hostili custodia liberet.
passages.english: Now let us return to the subject in hand. The wise man, even if he is content with himself, nevertheless wishes to have a friend, if for no other reason, in order to exercise friendship, so that so great a virtue may not lie idle; not for the purpose Epicurus stated in this very letter, that he may have someone to sit by him when he is sick and to help him when he is thrown into chains or is in want, but that he may have someone by whose sickbed he himself may sit, someone whom he himself may set free when beset by an enemy's guard.

passages.original: Nihilominus cum sit amicorum amantissimus, cum illos sibi comparet, saepe praeferat, omne intra se bonum terminabit et dicet, quod Stilbon ille dixit, Stilbon quem Epicuri epistula insequitur; hic enim capta patria, amissis liberis, amissa uxore cum ex incendio publico solus et tamen beatus exiret, interroganti Demetrio, cui cognomen ab exitio urbium Poliorcetes fuit, numquid perdidisset, Omnia, inquit, bona mea mecum sunt.
passages.english: Nonetheless, though he is the most loving of friends, though he ranks them equal to himself and often prefers them to himself, he will set the limit of all good within himself and will say what Stilbo said, that Stilbo whom Epicurus' letter attacks; for when his homeland had been captured, his children lost, his wife lost, and he was coming out of the general conflagration alone and yet happy, Demetrius, who got the surname Poliorcetes from his destruction of cities, asked him whether he had lost anything, and he said: "All my goods are with me."
passages.notes: Poliorcetes means 'Besieger of Cities'.

passages.original: Epicurus, inquis, dixit. Quid tibi cum alieno? Quod verum est, meum est. Perseverabo Epicurum tibi ingerere, ut isti, qui in verba iurant, nec quid dicatur aestimant, sed a quo, sciant, quae optima sunt, esse communia.
passages.english: "It was Epicurus," you say, "who said it. What have you to do with what belongs to another?" Whatever is true is mine. I shall go on pressing Epicurus upon you, so that those who swear by the words [of a master] and weigh not what is said but who says it may learn that the best things are common property.

passages.original: Cum hoc dicis, non videris vim ac potentiam eius, de quo cogitas, boni nosse. Et summam quidem rei pervides, quantum philosophia prosit, partes autem nondum satis subtiliter dispicis, necdum scis, quantum ubique nos adiuvet, quemadmodum et in maximis, ut Ciceronis utar verbo, opituletur et in minima descendat. Mihi crede, advoca illam in consilium; suadebit tibi, ne ad calculos sedeas.
passages.english: When you say this, you do not seem to me to know the force and power of the good you are thinking of. You do indeed grasp the sum of the matter, how much philosophy is of benefit, but you do not yet discern its parts closely enough, nor do you yet know how much it helps us everywhere, how it both gives aid in the greatest matters, to use Cicero's word, and descends to the smallest. Believe me, call it in to your counsel; it will advise you not to sit over your accounts.
passages.notes: Text appears to begin mid-argument; the referent of 'this' is not given.

passages.original: Ne gratis Idomeneus in epistulam meam venerit) ipse eam de suo redimet. Ad hunc Epicurus illam nobilem sententiam scripsit, qua hortatur, ut Pythoclea locupletem non publica nec ancipiti via faciat. Si vis, inquit, Pythoclea divitem facere, non pecuniae adiciendum, sed cupiditati detrahendum est.
passages.english: So that Idomeneus may not have entered my letter for nothing, he will pay for it himself out of his own resources. It was to him that Epicurus wrote that famous saying, in which he urges him to make Pythocles rich not by the common and risky road. "If you wish," he says, "to make Pythocles rich, you must not add to his money but take away from his desires."
passages.notes: A stray closing parenthesis after 'venerit' suggests the opening of the sentence is missing.

passages.original: divitiae paratae sunt. Aut gratuitum est, quo egemus, aut vile; panem et aquam natura desiderat Nemo ad haec pauper est, intra quae quisquis desiderium suum clusit, cum ipso Iove de felicitate contendat, ut ait Epicurus, cuius aliquam vocem huic epistulae involvam.
passages.english: riches are ready to hand. What we need is either free or cheap; nature wants bread and water. No one is poor with respect to these things, and whoever has confined his desire within them may contend with Jupiter himself for happiness, as Epicurus says, some saying of whom I will wrap into this letter.
passages.notes: Begins mid-sentence (preceded by 'Let us return to the law of nature;').

passages.original: Sic fac, inquit, omnia, tamquam spectet Epicurus. Prodest sine dubio custodem sibi inposuisse et habere, quem respicias, quem interesse cogitationibus tuis iudices. Hoc quidem longe magnificentius est, sic vivere tamquam sub alicuius boni viri ac semper praesentis oculis, sed ego etiam hoc contentus sum, ut sic facias, quaecumque facies, tamquam spectet aliquis;
passages.english: "Do everything," he says, "as if Epicurus were watching." There is no doubt it is beneficial to have set a guardian over oneself and to have someone to look back to, someone you consider present in your thoughts. It is indeed far nobler to live as if under the eyes of some good man who is always present, but I am content even with this, that whatever you do, you do it as if someone were watching;

passages.original: interim aliquorum te auctoritate custodi, aut Cato ille sit aut Scipio aut Laelius aut talis, cuius interventu perditi quoque homines vitia supprimerent, dum te efficis eum, cum quo peccare non audeas. Cum hoc effeceris, et aliqua coeperit apud te tui esse dignatio, incipiam tibi permittere, quod idem suadet Epicurus: Tunc praecipue in te ipse secede, cum esse cogeris in turba.
passages.english: Meanwhile, guard yourself by the authority of certain men, whether it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or someone of such a kind that at his arrival even abandoned men would suppress their vices, until you make yourself into a man in whose presence you would not dare to do wrong. When you have achieved this, and some respect for yourself has begun to take hold in you, I shall begin to allow you what Epicurus likewise advises: "Withdraw into yourself above all at the time when you are forced to be in a crowd."

passages.original: sed conficienda sunt sacra et huic epistulae viaticum dandum est. Puta me non dicere, unde sumpturus sum mutuum: scis cuius arca utar. Expecta me pusillum, et de domo fiet numeratio; interim commodabit Epicurus, qui ait: Meditare mortem vel si commodius sit transire ad deos.
passages.english: But the rites must be completed, and this letter must be given its travel-money. Suppose I do not say where I am going to borrow the loan from: you know whose strongbox I use. Wait for me a little, and the payment will be made from my own house; meanwhile Epicurus will lend [it], who says: "Rehearse death," or, if it is more convenient [put this way], "passing over to the gods."
passages.notes: The second half of the quotation is obscure and possibly corrupt; the sense seems to be that the same idea can be phrased as 'passing over to the gods'.

passages.original: Sed accipe iam quod debeo et vale. Divitiae sunt ad legem naturae conposita paupertas. Hoc saepe dicit Epicurus aliter atque aliter; sed numquam nimis dicitur, quod numquam satis discitur. Quibusdam remedia monstranda, quibusdam inculcanda sunt. Vale.
passages.english: But now receive what I owe, and farewell. Riches are poverty arranged according to the law of nature. Epicurus often says this in one way and another; but what is never sufficiently learned is never said too often. To some people remedies must be shown; on others they must be pressed home. Farewell.

passages.original: Hoc tibi soli putas accidisse et admirans quasi rem novam, quod peregrinatione tam longa et tot locorum varietatibus non discussisti tristitiam gravitatemque mentis? Animum debes mutare, non caelum. Licet vastum traieceris mare, licet, ut ait Vergilius noster, Terraeque urbesque recedant, sequentur te, quocumque perveneris, vitia.
passages.english: Do you think this has happened to you alone, and are you amazed, as if at something new, that by so long a journey and so many changes of place you have not shaken off the gloom and heaviness of your mind? You must change your mind, not your sky. Though you have crossed the vast sea, though, as our Virgil says, "lands and cities fall away," your vices will follow you wherever you arrive.

passages.original: Hoc idem querenti cuidam Socrates ait: Quid miraris nihil tibi peregrinationes prodesse, cum te circumferas? Premit te eadem causa, quae expulit. Quid terrarum iuvare novitas potest? Quid cognitio urbium aut locorum? In inritum cedit ista iactatio.
passages.english: When someone was making this same complaint, Socrates said: "Why are you surprised that your travels do you no good, when you carry yourself around with you? The same cause that drove you out weighs on you." What can the novelty of lands do to help? What can acquaintance with cities or places? That tossing about of yours comes to nothing.

passages.original: Dicebat quidem ille Epicuri praeceptis obsequens, primum sperare se nullum dolorem esse in illo extremo anhelitu; si tamen esset, habere aliquantum in ipsa brevitate solacii. Nullum enim dolorem longum esse, qui magnus est.
passages.english: He used to say, indeed, following the precepts of Epicurus, first that he hoped there was no pain in that last gasp; but if there were, that there was a good deal of comfort in its very brevity. For no pain is long that is great.

passages.original: Hoc dixit Zenon, hoc Cleanthes. Aliquid inter te intersit et librum. Quousque disces? Iam et praecipe. Quid est quare et audiam, quod legere possum?Multum, inquit, viva vox facit. Non quidem haec, quae alienis verbis commodatur et actuari vice fungitur.
passages.english: "This Zeno said, this Cleanthes said." Let there be some difference between you and a book. How long will you be learning? Now teach as well. What reason is there for me to hear what I can read? "The living voice," someone says, "does a great deal." Not, indeed, this one, which is lent to another's words and performs the function of a clerk.

passages.original: Plura enim veniunt quam quibus vox una sufficiat. Hoc non probo in philosopho, cuius pronuntiatio quoque, sicut vita, debet esse conposita; nihil autem ordinatum est, quod praecipitatur et properat. Itaque oratio illa apud Homerum concitata et sine intermissione in morem nivis superveniens iuveniori oratori data est, lenis et melle dulcior seni profluit.
passages.english: For more [words] come than a single voice is adequate for. I do not approve of this in a philosopher, whose delivery too, like his life, ought to be composed; and nothing is orderly that is hurled headlong and hurries. And so in Homer that rushing speech, coming on without pause like snow, is given to the younger orator; from the old man flows a gentle speech sweeter than honey.

passages.original: Quosdam ait Epicurus ad veritatem sine ullius adiutorio exisse, fecisse sibi ipsos viam. Hos maxime laudat, quibus ex se impetus fuit, qui se ipsi protulerunt. Quosdam indigere ope aliena, non ituros, si nemo praecesserit, sed bene secuturos.
passages.english: Epicurus says that some men have made their way out to the truth without anyone's help, and have made a road for themselves. These he praises most, who had the impulse from within themselves, who brought themselves forward. Others, [he says,] need another's aid: they will not go if no one has gone ahead, but they will follow well.

passages.original: Praeter haec adhuc invenies genus aliud hominum ne ipsum quidem fastidiendum eorum, qui cogi ad rectum conpellique possunt, quibus non duce tantum opus sit, sed adiutore et, ut ita dicam, coactore. Hic tertius color est. Si quaeris huius quoque exemplar, Hermarchum ait Epicurus talem fuisse. Itaque alteri magis gratulatur, alterum magis suspicit; quamvis enim ad eundem finem uterque pervenerit, tamen maior est laus idem effecisse in difficiliore materia.
passages.english: Besides these you will find yet another kind of men, not to be scorned either: those who can be forced and driven to what is right, who need not only a guide but a helper and, so to speak, a compeller. This is the third type. If you want an example of this too, Epicurus says that Hermarchus was such a man. And so he congratulates the one more, but admires the other more; for although both reached the same goal, yet the greater praise belongs to having achieved the same result with more difficult material.

passages.original: Etiam si exclamaveritis, non aliter audiam, quam si ad tactum vitiorum vestrorum ingemescatis. Testari vultis adtendere vos moverique magnitudine rerum? Sane liceat; ut quidem iudicetis et feratis de meliore suffragium, quidni non permittam? Apud Pythagoram discipulis quinque annis tacendum erat; numquid ergo existimas statim illis et loqui et laudare licuisse?
passages.english: Even if you shout out, I shall hear it no differently than if you were groaning at the touching of your vices. Do you wish to bear witness that you are attentive and moved by the greatness of the subject? Very well, let it be allowed; but that you should judge and cast your vote on what is better, why should I not refuse to permit? Under Pythagoras his disciples had to keep silent for five years; do you suppose, then, that they were allowed straightaway both to speak and to praise?
passages.notes: 'quidni non permittam' is awkward (literally 'why should I not not permit'); translated in the evident sense that Seneca refuses to let them pass judgement.

passages.original: Leve illud ingenium est nec sese adhuc reduxit introrsus, quod ad vocem et accidentia erigitur. Habet intus aliquid sollicitudinis et habet aliquid concepti pavoris, quod illum curiosum facit, ut ait Vergilius noster: Et me, quem dudum non ulla iniecta movebant Tela neque adverso glomerati ex agmine Grai,Nunc omnes terrent aurae, sonus excitat omnis Suspensum et pariter comitique onerique timentem.
passages.english: That mind is fickle, and has not yet withdrawn into itself, which is roused by a voice and by chance happenings. It has within it some anxiety and some fear already conceived, which makes it watchful, as our Virgil says: "And I, whom a while ago no weapons hurled at me could move, nor the Greeks massed in a hostile column, now am terrified by every breeze, every sound startles me, anxious and fearing alike for my companion and my burden."
passages.notes: The verses are Virgil, Aeneid 2.726–729 (Aeneas carrying Anchises and leading Ascanius).

passages.original: Dicebant antiqui si iusso, id est iussero. Hoc nolo mihi credas, sed eidem Vergilio: Cetera, qua iusso, mecum manus inferat arma.
passages.english: The ancients used to say "si iusso", that is, "iussero" ["if I shall have ordered"]. I do not want you to believe me on this, but the same Virgil: "Let the rest of the band bring in the arms with me, where I shall have ordered (iusso)."
passages.notes: The point is grammatical: the archaic form iusso for iussero; the verse is Aeneid 11.467.

passages.original: Non id ago nunc hac diligentia, ut ostendam, quantum tempus apud grammaticum perdiderim, sed ut ex hoc intellegas, quantum apud Ennium et Accium verborum situs occupaverit, cum apud hunc quoque, qui cotidie excutitur, aliqua nobis subducta sint.
passages.english: I am not taking such pains now in order to show how much time I wasted with the grammarian, but so that you may understand from this how much the mould of disuse has covered the words in Ennius and Accius, since even in this author too, who is pored over every day, some [words] have been taken from us.
passages.notes: 'Hunc' refers to an author (Virgil) discussed in the preceding, unsupplied context.

passages.original: Homo species est, ut Aristoteles ait; equus species est; canis species est; ergo commune aliquod quaerendum est his omnibus vinculum, quod illa conplectatur et sub se habeat. Hoc quid est? Animal. Ergo genus esse coepit horum omnium, quae modo rettuli, hominis, equi, canis, animal.
passages.english: Man is a species, as Aristotle says; a horse is a species; a dog is a species; therefore we must look for some common bond for all these, which embraces them and holds them under itself. What is this? Animal. So animal has come to be the genus of all those I just mentioned, man, horse, dog.

passages.original: Nunc ad id, quod tibi promisi, revertor, quomodo quaecumque sunt, in sex modos Plato partiatur. Primum illud quod est nec visu nec tactu nec ullo sensu conprenditur; cogitabile est. Quod generaliter est, tamquam homo generalis, sub oculos non venit; sed specialis venit, ut Cicero et Cato. Animal non videtur; cogitatur. Videtur autem species eius, equus et canis.
passages.english: Now I return to what I promised you: how Plato divides all things that exist into six modes. The first, "that which is", is grasped neither by sight nor by touch nor by any sense; it is thinkable. What exists generically, such as man in general, does not come before the eyes; but the particular does, such as Cicero and Cato. Animal is not seen; it is thought. But its species are seen, horse and dog.

passages.original: Secundum ex his, quae sunt, ponit Plato quod eminet et exsuperat omnia. Hoc ait per excellentiam esse. Poeta communiter dicitur, omnibus enim versus facientibus hoc nomen est, sed iam apud Graecos in unius notam cessit; Homerum intellegas, cum audieris poetam.
passages.english: Second among the things that exist Plato places that which stands out and surpasses all things. This, he says, exists by pre-eminence. "Poet" is said in a common sense, for all who make verses have this name, but among the Greeks it has now passed into the mark of one man; you understand Homer when you hear "the poet".

passages.original: Hoc est, quod ait Heraclitus: In idem flumen bis descendimus et non descendimus. Manet enim idem fluminis nomen, aqua transmissa est. Hoc in amne manifestius est quam in homine. Sed nos quoque non minus velox cursus praetervehit, et ideo admiror dementiam nostram, quod tantopere amamus rem fugacissimam, corpus, timemusque, ne quando moriamur, cum omne momentum mors prioris habitus sit.
passages.english: This is what Heraclitus says: "Into the same river we step twice and do not step." For the name of the river remains the same; the water has passed on. This is more evident in a river than in a man. But no less swift a course carries us along too, and therefore I wonder at our madness, that we so greatly love a most fleeting thing, the body, and fear that we may some day die, when every moment is the death of our previous state.

passages.original: Itaque cum dicit Vergilius noster Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie. Nullum enim malum gaudium est. Voluptatibus hoc nomen inposuit et quod voluit expressit. Significavit enim homines malo suo laetos.
passages.english: And so when our Virgil says "and the evil joys of the mind", he speaks eloquently indeed, but not quite precisely. For no joy is evil. He has put this name on pleasures and expressed what he meant: he meant people glad at their own harm.
passages.notes: Quotation from Aeneid 6.278–279.

passages.original: Hos itaque, ut ait Sallustius, ventri oboedientes animalium loco numeremus, non hominum, quosdam vero ne animalium quidem, sed mortuorum. Vivit is, qui multis usui est, vivit is, qui se utitur; qui vero latitant et torpent, sic in domo sunt, quomodo in conditivo.
passages.english: Let us therefore, as Sallust says, count these men who are obedient to their belly among animals, not men, and some indeed not even among animals, but among the dead. He lives who is of use to many; he lives who makes use of himself; but those who lurk and lie torpid are in their house as in a tomb.

passages.original: Stoicis placet unam causam esse, id, quod facit. Aristoteles putat causam tribus modis dici: Prima, inquit, causa est ipsa materia, sine qua nihil potest effici; secunda opifex. Tertia est forma, quae unicuique operi inponitur tamquam statuae; nam hanc Aristoteles idos vocat.
passages.english: The Stoics hold that there is one cause, that which makes. Aristotle thinks "cause" is spoken of in three ways: "The first cause," he says, "is the matter itself, without which nothing can be produced; the second, the maker. The third is the form, which is imposed on each work, as on a statue"; for this Aristotle calls the *idos* [form].
passages.notes: idos = Greek eidos.

passages.original: His quintam Plato adicit exemplar, quam ipse idean vocat; hoc est enim, ad quod respiciens artifex id, quod destinabat, effecit. Nihil autem ad rem pertinet, utrum foris habeat exemplar, ad quod referat oculos, an intus, quod ibi ipse concepit et posuit.
passages.english: To these Plato adds a fifth, the model, which he himself calls the *idea*; for this is what the craftsman looks to in producing what he intended. And it makes no difference whether he has the model outside, to which he can turn his eyes, or inside, which he himself conceived and set there.

passages.original: Quinque ergo causae sunt, ut Plato dicit: id ex quo, id a quo, id in quo, id ad quod, id propter quod. Novissime id quod ex his est. Tamquam in statua, quia de hac loqui coepimus, id ex quo aes est, id a quo artifex est, id in quo forma est, quae aptatur illi, id ad quod exemplar est, quod imitatur is, qui facit, id propter quod facientis propositum est, id quod ex istis est, ipsa statua est.
passages.english: So there are five causes, as Plato says: that from which, that by which, that in which, that toward which, that for the sake of which. Last of all, that which results from these. As in a statue, since we began to speak of this: that from which is the bronze; that by which is the artist; that in which is the form that is fitted to it; that toward which is the model which the maker imitates; that for the sake of which is the maker's purpose; that which results from these is the statue itself.

passages.original: Haec omnia mundus quoque, ut ait Plato, habet: facientem: hic deus est. Ex quo fit: haec materia est. Formam: haec est habitus et ordo mundi, quem videmus. Exemplar, scilicet, ad quod deus hanc magnitudinem operis pulcherrimi fecit.
passages.english: The world too, as Plato says, has all these: a maker, and this is god; that from which it is made, and this is matter; a form, and this is the shape and order of the world which we see; a model, namely that according to which god made this vast and most beautiful work.

passages.original: Propositum, propter quod fecit. Quaeris, quod sit propositum deo? Bonitas. Ita certe Plato ait: Quae deo faciendi mundum fuit causa? Bonus est; bono nulla cuiusquam boni invidia est. Fecit itaque quam optimum potuit. Fer ergo, iudex, sententiam et pronuntia, quis tibi videatur verissimum dicere, non quis verissimum dicat.
passages.english: [It has] a purpose, for the sake of which he made it. Do you ask what god's purpose is? Goodness. So at any rate Plato says: "What was god's reason for making the world? He is good; the good feel no grudging toward any good thing. So he made it as good as he could." Cast your vote, then, judge, and pronounce who seems to you to speak most truly, not who does speak most truly.

passages.original: Scio, quid mihi responderi hoc loco possit: hoc nobis persuadere conaris, nihil interesse, utrum aliquis in gaudio sit an in eculeo iaceat ac tortorem suum lasset? Poteram respondere: Epicurus quoque ait sapientem, si in Phalaridis tauro peruratur, exclamaturum: dulce est et ad me nihil pertinet. Quid miraris, si ego paria bona dico alterius in convivio iacentis, alterius inter tormenta fortissime stantis, cum quod incredibilius est dicat Epicurus, dulce esse torreri?
passages.english: I know what can be answered to me at this point: "Are you trying to persuade us that it makes no difference whether someone is in joy or lies on the rack and wears out his torturer?" I could answer: Epicurus too says that the wise man, if he is burned in the bull of Phalaris, will cry out: "It is pleasant, and it does not concern me at all." Why are you surprised if I say that the goods of one man reclining at a banquet and of another standing most bravely amid tortures are equal, when Epicurus says what is more incredible, that it is pleasant to be roasted?

passages.original: Nec est, quare hoc inter nostra placita mireris; apud Epicurum duo bona sunt, ex quibus summum illud beatumque conponitur, ut corpus sine dolore sit, animus sine perturbatione. Haec bona non crescunt, si plena sunt. Quo enim crescet, quod plenum est? Dolore corpus caret;
passages.english: Nor is there reason for you to be surprised at this among our doctrines; for Epicurus there are two goods, from which that supreme and blessed [good] is composed: that the body be free from pain and the mind free from disturbance. These goods do not increase if they are complete. For to what will something increase which is complete? The body is free from pain;

passages.original: Dabo apud Epicurum tibi etiamnunc simillimam huic nostrae divisionem bonorum. Alia enim sunt apud illum, quae malit contingere sibi, ut corporis quietem ab omni incommodo liberam et animi remissionem bonorum suorum contemplatione gaudentis.
passages.english: I will give you further, in Epicurus, a division of goods very similar to this one of ours. For there are some things with him which he would prefer to befall him, such as rest of the body free from every discomfort, and relaxation of a mind rejoicing in the contemplation of its own goods.

passages.original: Ergo et apud Epicurum sunt haec bona, quae malles non experiri, sed quia ita res tulit, et amplexanda et laudanda et exaequanda summis sunt. Non potest dici, hoc non esse par maximis bonum, quod beatae vitae clausulam inposuit, cui Epicurus extrema voce gratias egit.
passages.english: So in Epicurus too there are these goods which you would prefer not to experience, but because circumstances have brought it so, they must be embraced and praised and made equal to the highest. It cannot be said that this is not a good equal to the greatest, which set the closing seal on a happy life and to which Epicurus gave thanks with his last words.

passages.original: Praenavigavimus, Lucili, vitam et quemadmodum in mari, ut ait Vergilius noster, Terraeque urbesque recedant, sic in hoc cursu rapidissimi temporis primum pueritiam abscondimus, deinde adulescentiam, deinde quidquid est illud inter iuvenem et senem medium, in utriusque confinio positum, deinde ipsius senectutis optimos annos.
passages.english: We have sailed past life, Lucilius, and just as at sea, as our Vergil says, "lands and cities recede," so in this course of most swiftly running time we first lose sight of boyhood, then youth, then whatever that is between young man and old, placed on the border of both, then the best years of old age itself.
passages.notes: "Praenavigavimus" (sailed past) may be read as rhetorical; the quotation is from Aeneid 3.72.

passages.original: Non est ergo M. Catonis maius bonum honesta vita quam mors honesta, quoniam non intenditur virtus. Idem esse dicebat Socrates veritatem et virtutem. Quomodo illa non crescit, sic ne virtus quidem; habet numeros suos, plena est.
passages.english: Therefore an honourable life is not a greater good for Marcus Cato than an honourable death, since virtue is not increased. Socrates used to say that truth and virtue are the same. Just as truth does not grow, so neither does virtue; it has its full measure, it is complete.

passages.original: His te cogitationibus recrea et interim epistulis nostris vaca. Veniet aliquando tempus, quod nos iterum iungat ac misceat; quantulumlibet sit illud, longum faciet scientia utendi. Nam, ut Posidonius ait, unus dies hominum eruditorum plus patet quam inperitis longissima aetas.
passages.english: Refresh yourself with these thoughts, and in the meantime devote yourself to our letters. A time will come at some point that will join and unite us again; however short it may be, knowing how to use it will make it long. For, as Posidonius says, a single day of educated men extends further than the longest lifetime of the unskilled.

passages.original: Apes, ut aiunt, debemus imitari, quae vagantur et flores ad mel faciendum idoneos carpunt, deinde quicquid attulere, disponunt ac per favos digerunt et, ut Vergilius noster ait, liquentia mella Stipant et dulci distendunt nectare cellas.
passages.english: We ought, as they say, to imitate the bees, which roam about and pluck the flowers suited to making honey, then arrange whatever they have brought and distribute it through the combs, and, as our Vergil says, "pack the flowing honey and swell the cells with sweet nectar."
passages.notes: Quotation from Aeneid 1.432–433.

passages.original: Descripturus infamem et nimiis notabilem deliciis Horatius Flaccus quid ait? Pastillos Buccillus olet. Dares nunc Buccillum; proinde esset ac si hircum oleret, Gargonii loco esset, quem idem Horatius Buccillo opposuit. Parum est sumere unguentum, nisi bis die terque renovatur, ne evanescat in corpore.
passages.english: When Horace Flaccus is about to describe a man of ill repute, conspicuous for excessive luxury, what does he say? "Buccillus smells of lozenges." Produce a Buccillus now: he would be as if he smelled of a goat; he would be in the place of Gargonius, whom the same Horace set against Buccillus. It is not enough to put on perfume unless it is renewed twice or three times a day, so that it does not fade away on the body.
passages.notes: Horace's line (Satires 1.2.27, 1.4.92) is usually "Pastillos Rufillus olet"; the text here reads "Buccillus", which I have kept.

passages.original: Te quoque proteget illa, quae Tarda venit seris factura nepotibus umbram, ut ait Vergilius noster, qui non quid verissime, sed quid decentissime diceretur aspexit nec agricolas docere voluit, sed legentes delectare.
passages.english: You too will be shaded by that tree which "comes slowly, to make shade for distant grandchildren," as our Virgil says, who looked not to what would be said most truly, but to what would be said most fittingly, and wished not to teach farmers, but to delight readers.
passages.notes: Quotation from Virgil, Georgics 2.58.

passages.original: Posidonius, ut ego existimo, melius, qui ait divitias esse causam malorum, non quia ipsae faciunt aliquid, sed quia facturos inritant. Alia est enim causa e(iiciens, quae protinus necesse est noceat, alia praecedens. Hanc praecedentem causam divitiae habent;
passages.english: Posidonius, in my opinion, [speaks] better, who says that riches are a cause of evils, not because they themselves do anything, but because they provoke those who are going to do [evil]. For an efficient cause, which must necessarily do harm at once, is one thing; an antecedent cause is another. Riches are a cause of this antecedent kind;
passages.notes: 'e(iiciens' is a scanning error for 'efficiens' (efficient).

passages.original: Posidonius sic interrogandum ait: quae neque magnitudinem animo dant nec fiduciam nec securitatem, non sunt bona. Divitiae autem et bona valetudo et similia his nihil horum faciunt; ergo non sunt bona. Hanc interrogationem magis etiam nunc hoc modo intendit: quae neque magnitudinem animo dant nec fiduciam nec securitatem, contra autem insolentiam, tumorem, arrogantiam creant, mala sunt.
passages.english: Posidonius says the argument should be put this way: things that give the mind neither greatness nor confidence nor freedom from care are not goods. But riches and good health and things like them do none of these; therefore they are not goods. He presses this argument still further in this way: things that give the mind neither greatness nor confidence nor freedom from care, but on the contrary create insolence, conceit and arrogance, are evils.

passages.original: unus tibi nodus, sed Herculaneus restat: ex malis bonum non fit. Ex multis paupertatibus divitiae fiunt; ergo divitiae bonum non sunt. Hanc interrogationem nostri non agnoscunt, Peripatetici et fingunt illam et solvunt. Ait autem Posidonius hoc sophisma, per omnes dialecticorum scholas iactatum, sic ab Antipatro refelli:
passages.english: One knot remains for you, but a Herculean one: good does not come from evils. Riches come from many poverties; therefore riches are not a good. Our [Stoics] do not recognise this argument; the Peripatetics both invent it and solve it. Posidonius says, moreover, that this sophism, bandied about through all the schools of the dialecticians, is refuted by Antipater as follows:
passages.notes: Punctuation of 'nostri non agnoscunt, Peripatetici' is uncertain; it may also read 'our school does not recognise it; the Peripatetics both frame it and resolve it'.

passages.original: Quattuor ait esse artium Posidonius genera: sunt volgares et sordidae, sunt ludicrae, sunt pueriles, sunt liberales. Volgares opificum, quae manu constant et ad instruendam vitam occupatae sunt, in quibus nulla decoris, nulla honesti simulatio est.
passages.english: Posidonius says there are four kinds of arts: there are the common and base, there are those of entertainment, there are those for boys, there are the liberal. The common are those of workmen, which consist in handwork and are busied with furnishing life's needs, in which there is no pretence of beauty or of honour.

passages.original: Apion grammaticus, qui sub C. Caesare tota circulatus est Graecia et in nomen Homeri ab omnibus civitatibus adoptatus, aiebat Homerum utraque materia consummata, et Odyssia et Iliade, principium adiecisse operi suo, quo bellum Troianum complexus est. Huius rei argumentum adferebat, quod duas litteras in primo versu posuisset ex industria librorum suorum numerum continentes.
passages.english: Apion the grammarian, who in the time of Gaius Caesar toured all Greece and was adopted by every city in the name of Homer, used to say that Homer, after completing both his subjects, the Odyssey and the Iliad, added a beginning to his work, in which he embraced the Trojan War. As proof of this he offered the fact that he had deliberately placed in the first line two letters containing the number of his books.
passages.notes: The two letters are presumably μῆνιν's opening μ and η, read as numerals 40 + 8 = 48, the combined books of the two poems.

passages.original: Audi, quantum mali faciat nimia subtilitas et quam infesta veritati sit. Protagoras ait de omni re in utramque partem disputari posse ex aequo et de hac ipsa, an omnis res in utramque partem disputabilis sit. Nausiphanes ait ex his, quae videntur esse, nihil magis esse quam non esse.
passages.english: Hear how much harm excessive subtlety does and how hostile it is to truth. Protagoras says that on every matter one can argue on either side with equal force, and also on this very question, whether every matter can be argued on either side. Nausiphanes says that of the things that seem to exist, none exists more than it does not exist.

passages.original: Parmenides ait ex his, quae videntur, nihil esse uno excepto universo. Zenon Eleates omnia negotia de negotio deiecit: ait nihil esse. Circa eadem fere Pyrrhonei versantur et Megarici et Eretrici et Academici, qui novam induxerunt scientiam, nihil scire.
passages.english: Parmenides says that of the things that appear, nothing exists except the One, the universe. Zeno of Elea threw all the trouble out of the trouble: he says that nothing exists. The Pyrrhonists, the Megarians, the Eretrians and the Academics are concerned with roughly the same things; they have introduced a new knowledge: to know nothing.
passages.notes: "omnia negotia de negotio deiecit" is a wordplay, roughly "got rid of all difficulty by getting rid of everything"; sense uncertain.

passages.original: Illo ergo saeculo, quod aureum perhibent, penes sapientes fuisse regnum Posidonius iudicat. Hi continebant manus et infirmiorem a validioribus tuebantur, suadebant dissuadebantque et utilia atque inutilia monstrabant. Horum prudentia ne quid deesset suis providebat, fortitudo pericula arcebat, beneficentia augebat ornabatque subiectos.
passages.english: In that age, then, which they call golden, Posidonius judges that rule lay in the hands of the wise. They kept [men's] hands in check and protected the weaker from the stronger; they urged and dissuaded, and pointed out what was useful and what useless. Their foresight provided that their people should lack nothing, their courage warded off dangers, their beneficence enriched and adorned their subjects.

passages.original: Non abduxit, inquam, se, ut Posidonio videtur, ab istis artibus sapiens, sed ad illas omnino non venit. Nihil enim dignum inventu iudicasset, quod non erat dignum perpetuo usu iudicaturus. Ponenda non sumeret.
passages.english: The wise man did not, I say, withdraw himself from those arts, as Posidonius thinks; rather, he never came to them at all. For he would have judged nothing worth discovering which he was not going to judge worth using permanently. He would not take up things that would have to be laid down.

passages.original: Anacharsis, inquit, invenit rotam figuli, cuius circuitu vasa formantur. Deinde quia apud Homerum invenitur figuli rota, malunt videri versus falsos esse quam fabulam. Ego nec Anacharsim auctorem huius rei fuisse contendo et, si fuit, sapiens quidem hoc invenit, sed non tamquam sapiens, sicut multa sapientes faciunt, qua homines sunt, non qua sapientes.
passages.english: "Anacharsis," he says, "invented the potter's wheel, by whose turning vessels are shaped." Then, because the potter's wheel is found in Homer, they prefer that the verses be thought spurious rather than the story. I do not maintain that Anacharsis was the originator of this thing, and, if he was, a wise man did indeed invent it, but not as a wise man, just as wise men do many things in so far as they are men, not in so far as they are wise.

passages.original: Democritus, inquit, invenisse dicitur fornicem, ut lapidum curvatura paulatim inclinatorum medio saxo alligaretur. Hoc dicam falsum esse; necesse est enim ante Democritum et pontes et portas fuisse, quarum fere summa curvantur.
passages.english: "Democritus," he says, "is said to have invented the arch, so that the curve of stones gradually inclined would be bound together by a keystone in the middle." This I will call false; for there must have been, before Democritus, both bridges and gateways, whose tops are usually curved.

passages.original: Huic rationem servire iusserunt et fecerunt animalis generosissimi summum bonum demissum et ignobile, praeterea mixtum portentosumque et ex diversis ac male congruentibus membris. Nam ut ait Vergilius noster in Scylla Prima hominis facies et pulchro pectore virgo Pube tenus, postrema inmani corpore pistrix Delphinum caudas utero commissa luporum. Huic tamen Scyllae fera animalia adiuncta sunt, horrenda, velocia; at isti sapientiam ex quibus conposuere portentis!
passages.english: They have ordered reason to serve this, and have made the highest good of the noblest living creature something low and ignoble, and besides something mixed and monstrous, made of diverse and ill-fitting limbs. For as our Virgil says of Scylla: "Above, a human face, and a maiden with lovely breast down to the groin; below, a sea-monster of enormous body, with dolphins' tails joined to a belly of wolves." Yet to this Scylla wild animals are attached, fearsome and swift; but out of what monstrosities have these men composed wisdom!
passages.notes: "Huic" refers to pleasure (from the lost preceding context). Quotation from Aeneid 3.426–428.

passages.original: Prima ars hominis est ipsa virtus; huic committitur inutilis caro et fluida, receptandis tantum cibis habilis, ut ait Posidonius. Virtus illa divina in lubricum desinit et superioribus eius partibus venerandis atque caelestibus animal iners ac marcidum adtexitur. Illa utcumque altera quies nihil quidem ipsa praestabat animo, sed inpedimenta removebat;
passages.english: The first art of man is virtue itself; to it is joined useless and flabby flesh, fit only for taking in food, as Posidonius says. That divine virtue ends in something slippery, and to its upper parts, which are venerable and heavenly, a sluggish and flaccid animal is attached. That other thing, quiet, whatever it was, contributed nothing to the mind itself, but it did remove hindrances;
passages.notes: The passage appears to be dislocated or corrupt; the attribution to Posidonius and the sense of 'altera quies' are uncertain. The text seems to blend phrases from different parts of Seneca's letters.

passages.original: Maiestatem enim eius ex nostra inbecillitate metimur et vitiis nostris nomen virtutis inponimus. Quid porro? Non aeque incredibile videtur aliquem in summis cruciatibus positum dicere beatus sum? Atqui haec vox in ipsa officina voluptatis audita est. Beatissimum, inquit, hunc et hunc diem ago Epicurus, cum illum hinc urinae difficultas torqueret, hinc insanabilis exulcerati dolor ventris.
passages.english: For we measure its greatness by our own weakness, and we put the name of virtue on our vices. What next? Does it not seem equally incredible that someone placed in the utmost torments should say, "I am happy"? And yet this utterance was heard in the very workshop of pleasure. "This day, and this one," says Epicurus, "I am spending as most happy," when on one side difficulty in passing urine was torturing him, and on the other the incurable pain of an ulcerated stomach.
passages.notes: "eius" refers to virtue.

passages.original: In hac re dissentio a Posidonio, qui inprobo, inquit, quod Platonis legibus adiecta principia sunt. Legem enim brevem esse oportet, quo facilius ab imperitis teneatur. Velut emissa divinitus vox sit; iubeat, non disputet. Nihil videtur mihi frigidius, nihil ineptius quam lex cum prologo.
passages.english: On this point I disagree with Posidonius, who says: "I disapprove of the fact that preambles have been added to Plato's laws. For a law ought to be brief, so that it may be grasped more easily by the unlearned. Let it be like a voice sent from heaven; let it command, not argue. Nothing seems to me more frigid, nothing more inept, than a law with a prologue."

passages.original: Quorsus, inquis, hoc pertinet? Aeque praecepta bona, si saepe tecum sint, profutura quam bona exempla. Pythagoras ait alium animum fieri intrantibus templum deorumque simulacra ex vicino cernentibus et alicuius oraculi opperientibus vocem.
passages.english: "What is the point of this?" you ask. That good precepts, if they are often with you, will be as beneficial as good examples. Pythagoras says that a different mind comes over those who enter a temple and see the images of the gods close at hand and wait for the voice of some oracle.

passages.original: Nam tibi de summa caeli ratione deumque Disserere incipiam et rerum primordia pandam;Unde omnis natura creet res, auctet alatque,Quoque eadem rursus natura perempta resolvat, ut ait Lucretius. Sequitur ergo ut, cum contemplativa sit, habeat decreta sua.
passages.english:
"For I will begin to discourse to you on the highest system of the heaven and the gods,
and will unfold the first beginnings of things,
from which nature creates all things, increases and nourishes them,
and into which the same nature resolves them again when they perish,"
as Lucretius says. It follows, then, that since [philosophy] is contemplative, it has its own doctrines.
passages.notes: Lucretius 1.54–57.

passages.original: His adicit causarum inquisitionem, aetiologian quam quare nos dicere non audeamus, cum grammatici, custodes Latini sermonis, suo iure ita appellent, non video. Ait utilem futuram et descriptionem cuiusque virtutis; hanc Posidonius ethologian vocat, quidam characterismon appellant, signa cuiusque virtutis ac vitii et notas reddentem, quibus inter se similia discriminentur.
passages.english: To these he adds the investigation of causes, *aetiologia* [aetiology], and I do not see why we should not dare to say this, since the grammarians, guardians of the Latin language, call it so by their own right. He says that a description of each virtue will also be useful; this Posidonius calls *ethologia* [character-description], some call it *characterismos*, giving the signs and marks of each virtue and vice by which things similar to one another may be distinguished.
passages.notes: The opening clause on aetiologia may be garbled; the sense 'why we should not dare to say [it]' is inferred.

passages.original: Illic dissentiamus cum Epicuro, ubi dicit nihil iustum esse natura et crimina vitanda esse, quia vitari metus non posse; hic consentiamus mala facinora conscientia flagellari et plurimum illi tormentorum esse eo, quod perpetua illam sollicitudo urget ac verberat, quod sponsoribus securitatis suae non potest credere.
passages.english: Let us disagree with Epicurus there, where he says that nothing is just by nature and that crimes are to be avoided because fears cannot be avoided; here let us agree that evil deeds are scourged by conscience, and that its greatest torment lies in this, that perpetual anxiety presses and lashes it, and that it cannot trust the guarantors of its own security.

passages.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis. At contra Pollionis Asinii salebrosa et exiliens et ubi minime exspectes, relictura. Denique omnia apud Ciceronem desinunt, aput Pollionem cadunt exceptis paucissimis, quae ad certum modum et ad unum exemplar adstricta sunt.
passages.english: Read Cicero: his composition is uniform; it bends its foot slowly, and it is soft without disgrace. But that of Asinius Pollio, by contrast, is rugged and jumpy, and will leave off where you least expect it. In short, in Cicero everything comes to a close, in Pollio everything falls, except for a very few [passages] which are bound to a fixed rhythm and to a single pattern.
passages.notes: 'pedem curvat lenta' is an obscure phrase, apparently referring to the rhythmical movement of Cicero's prose. Some editions read 'gradu' or similar here.

passages.original: Dic Ciceronem, cuius libri ad philosophiam pertinentes paene totidem sunt, quot Fabiani; cedam, sed non statim pusillum est, si quid maximo minus est. Dic Asinium Pollionem; cedam, et respondeamus: in re tanta eminere est post duos esse. Nomina adhuc. T. Livium, scripsit enim et dialogos, quos non magis philosophiae adnumerare possis quam historiae, et ex professo philosophiam continentis libros; huic quoque dabo locum. Vide tamen, quam multos antecedat, qui a tribus vincitur et tribus eloquentissimis.
passages.english: Name Cicero, whose books relating to philosophy are almost as many as Fabianus'. I will yield, but it is not straightway small if something is less than the greatest. Name Asinius Pollio. I will yield, and let us answer: in so great a matter, to stand out is to come after two. Name still others. Titus Livius, for he too wrote dialogues, which you could no more count as philosophy than as history, and books that avowedly contain philosophy; to him also I will give place. But see how many a man surpasses who is beaten by three, and by three most eloquent men.
passages.notes: 'continentis' is presumably for 'continentes'.

passages.original: Quid huic optes nisi deos faciles? Quid sibi vult ista carminis effeminati turpitudo? Quid timoris dementissimi pactio? Quid tam foeda vitae mendicatio? Huic putes umquam recitasse Vergilium: Usque adeone mori miserum est? Optat ultima malorum, et quae pati gravissimum est extendi ac sustineri cupit; qua mercede? Scilicet vitae longioris. Quod autem vivere est diu mori?
passages.english: What would you wish for such a man except gods who are easy [to grant prayers]? What is the meaning of this disgraceful, effeminate poem? What of this bargain struck by the most insane fear? What of so foul a begging for life? You would think Virgil had never read aloud to him: 'Is it so very wretched to die?' He wishes for the worst of evils, and longs for what is hardest to bear to be prolonged and endured. For what reward? Of course, a longer life. But what sort of living is a long dying?
passages.notes: 'recitasse' might rather mean that the man himself had never read Virgil aloud; the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: Vive cum Chrysippo, cum Posidonio: hi tibi tradent humanorum divinorumque notitiam, hi iubebunt in opere esse nec tantum scite loqui et in oblectationem audientium verba iactare, sed animum indurare et adversus minas erigere. Unus est enim huius vitae fluctuantis et turbidae portus eventura contemnere, stare fidenter ac paratum tela fortunae adverso pectore excipere, non latitantem nec tergiversantem.
passages.english: Live with Chrysippus, with Posidonius: these will give you knowledge of things human and divine; these will bid you be at work, and not merely speak cleverly and toss out words for the delight of listeners, but harden your mind and raise it up against threats. For the one harbour of this tossing and turbulent life is to despise what is to come, to stand confidently and ready, receiving the weapons of fortune with your breast facing them, not hiding or turning your back.

passages.original: itaque nulli se rei summittat, nihil illi videatur grave, nihil quod virum incurvet. Terribiles visu formae letumque labosque; minime quidem, si quis rectis oculis intueri illa possit et tenebras perrumpere. Multa per noctem habita terrori dies vertit ad risum. Terribiles visu formae letumque labosque: egregie Vergilius noster non re dixit terribiles esse, sed visu, id est videri, non esse.
passages.english: and so let him submit to nothing; let nothing seem heavy to him, nothing that would bow a man down. 'Shapes terrible to see, both death and toil': not at all, if one could look at them with a steady gaze and break through the darkness. Many things held to be terrifying during the night are turned to laughter by the day. 'Shapes terrible to see, both death and toil': our Virgil put it excellently in saying that they are terrible not in fact but 'to see', that is, that they seem [terrible], not that they are.

passages.original: Numquid est dubium, an id, quo quid tangi potest, corpus sit? Tangere enim et tangi nisi corpus nulla potest res, ut ait Lucretius. Omnia autem ista, quae dixi, non mutarent corpus, nisi tangerent; ergo corpora sunt.
passages.english: Is there any doubt whether that by which something can be touched is a body? 'For nothing can touch or be touched unless it is body,' as Lucretius says. Moreover, all those things I have mentioned would not change the body unless they touched it; therefore they are bodies.

passages.original: Et sic adloquamur Iovem, cuius gubernaculo moles ista derigitur, quemadmodum Cleanthes noster versibus disertissimis adloquitur, quos mihi in nostrum sermonem mutare permittitur Ciceronis, disertissimi viri, exemplo. Si placuerint, boni consules; si displicuerint, scies me in hoc secutum Ciceronis exemplum:
passages.english: And so let us address Jupiter, by whose helm this mass [of the universe] is steered, as our Cleanthes addresses him in most eloquent verses, which I am permitted to turn into our language following the example of Cicero, a most eloquent man. If they please you, take them in good part; if they displease you, you will know that in this I have followed Cicero's example:

passages.original: Nam, ut dicebat Cleanthes, quemadmodum spiritus noster clariorem sonum reddit, cum illum tuba per longi canalis angustias tractum patentiore novissime exitu effudit, sic sensus nostros clariores carminis arta necessitas efficit. Eadem neglegentius audiuntur minusque percutiunt, quamdiu soluta oratione dicuntur; ubi accessere numeri et egregium sensum adstrinxere certi pedes, eadem illa sententia velut lacerto excussiore torquetur.
passages.english: For, as Cleanthes used to say, just as our breath gives a clearer sound when a trumpet has drawn it through the narrows of a long tube and poured it out at last through a wider opening, so the tight constraint of verse makes our thoughts clearer. The same things are heard more carelessly and strike less forcefully as long as they are said in prose; when metre has been added and fixed feet have bound up a fine thought, that same idea is hurled as if by a more vigorous arm.

passages.original: At Pythagoras omnium inter omnia cognationem esse dicebat et animorum commercium in alias atque alias formas transeuntium. Nulla, si illi credas, anima interit, ne cessat quidem nisi tempore exiguo, dum in aliud corpus transfunditur. videbimus, per quas temporum vices et quando pererratis pluribus domiciliis in hominem revertatur;
passages.english: But Pythagoras used to say that there is a kinship of all things with all things, and an interchange of souls passing into one form after another. No soul, if you believe him, perishes; it does not even cease, except for a brief time, while it is being poured over into another body. We shall see through what turns of time, and when, after wandering through many dwellings, it returns into a human being;

passages.original: Qui grammaticus futurus Vergilium scrutatur, non hoc animo legit illud egregium: fugit inreparabile tempus: vigilandum est; nisi properamus, relinquemur; agit nos agiturque velox dies; inscii rapimur; omnia in futurum disponimus et inter praecipitia lenti sumus; sed ut observet, quotiens Vergilius de celeritate temporum dicit, hoc uti verbo illum fugit.Optima quaeque dies miseris mortalibus aevi Prima fugit; subeunt morbi tristisque senectus Et labor, et durae rapit inclementia mortis.
passages.english: The man who, intending to be a grammarian, examines Virgil does not read that excellent line 'time flies irretrievably' in this spirit: 'We must be watchful; unless we hurry, we shall be left behind; the swift day drives us and is driven; we are swept along unawares; we arrange everything for the future, and amid the headlong rush we are slow.' Rather, [he reads it] in order to note that whenever Virgil speaks of the swiftness of time, he uses this verb 'flies': 'Each best day of life for wretched mortals flies first; diseases come on, and gloomy old age, and toil, and the harshness of unyielding death sweeps them away.'
passages.notes: In the final line 'rapit' has no expressed object; 'them' is supplied.

passages.original: Ille, qui ad philosophiam spectat, haec eadem quo debet, adducit: numquam Vergilius, inquit, dies dicit ire, sed fugere, quod currendi genus concitatissimum est, et optimos quosque primos rapi; quid ergo cessamus nos ipsi concitare, ut velocitatem rapidissimae rei possimus aequare? Meliora praetervolant, deteriora succedunt.
passages.english: He who looks towards philosophy brings these same words to where he ought. 'Virgil never,' he says, 'says that days go, but that they flee, which is the most headlong kind of running, and that all the best are snatched away first. Why then do we delay to spur ourselves on, so that we can match the speed of the swiftest of things? The better things fly past, the worse take their place.'

passages.original: Haec non cogitat ille, qui grammatici oculis carmen istud legit, ideo optimum quemque primum esse diem, quia subeunt morbi, quia senectus premit et adhuc adulescentiam cogitantibus supra caput est; sed ait Vergilium semper una ponere morbos et senectutem, non mehercules immerito. Senectus enim insanabilis morbus est.
passages.english: The man who reads this poem with a grammarian's eyes does not reflect that every best day is the first for this reason: that diseases come on, that old age presses upon us and is already over the heads of those who are still thinking of their youth. Instead he says that Virgil always puts diseases and old age together, and not without reason, by Hercules. For old age is an incurable disease.

passages.original: Eosdem libros cum grammaticus explicuit, primum verba expressa, reapse dici a Cicerone, id est re ipsa, in commentarium refert, nec minus sepse, id est se ipse. Deinde transit ad ea, quae consuetudo saeculi mutavit, tamquam ait Cicero: quoniam sumus ab ipsa calce eius interpellatione revocati. Hanc quam nunc in circo cretam vocamus, calcem antiqui dicebant.
passages.english: When a grammarian has explained these same books, he first enters in his commentary the words used, that *reapse* is said by Cicero, that is *re ipsa* ["in reality"], and no less *sepse*, that is *se ipse* ["himself"]. Then he passes on to those things which the usage of the age has changed, as when Cicero says: "since we have been called back by his interruption from the very *calx*." What we now call the chalk line in the circus, the ancients called the *calx*.
passages.notes: *calx* (lime, chalk) here denotes the finishing line of the race-course; the Latin also has *creta* (chalk) for the modern term.

passages.original: Deinde Ennianos colligit versus et in primis illos de Africano scriptos: cui nemo civis neque hostis Quibit pro factis reddere opis pretium. Ex eo se ait intellegere, opem aput antiquos non tantum auxilium significasse, sed operam. Ait enim Ennius neminem potuisse Scipioni neque civem neque hostem reddere operae pretium.
passages.english: Then he collects verses of Ennius, and above all those written about Africanus: "to whom no citizen nor enemy could render the price of help for his deeds." From this he says he understands that among the ancients *ops* signified not only aid but effort. For Ennius says that no one, neither citizen nor enemy, could have rendered Scipio the price of his effort.

passages.original: Felicem deinde se putat, quod invenerit, unde visum sit Vergilio dicere: quem super ingens porta tonat caeli. Ennium hoc ait Homero subripuisse, Ennio vergilium. Esse enim apud Ciceronem in his ipsis de Re Publica hoc epigramma Enni: Si fas endo plagas caelestum ascendere cuiquam est,Mi soli caeli maxima porta patet.
passages.english: Then he thinks himself fortunate to have found the source from which Virgil saw fit to say: "above whom the huge gate of heaven thunders." He says Ennius stole this from Homer, and Virgil from Ennius. For in Cicero, in these very books On the Republic, there is this epigram of Ennius: "If it is right for anyone to ascend into the regions of the heavenly ones, for me alone the greatest gate of heaven lies open."

passages.original: Omnia quae dicunt, quae turba audiente iactant, aliena sunt; dixit illa Platon, dixit Zenon, dixit Chrysippus et Posidonius et ingens agmen nostrorum tot ac talium. Quomodo probare possint sua esse, monstrabo: faciant, quae dixerint.
passages.english: Everything they say, everything they toss out while the crowd listens, belongs to others: Plato said it, Zeno said it, Chrysippus and Posidonius said it, and the huge column of our school, so many and such men. I will show how they can prove these things are their own: let them do what they have said.

passages.original: Quid vocentur Latine sophismata, quaesisti a me. Multi temptaverunt illis nomen inponere, nullum haesit, videlicet, quia res ipsa non recipiebatur a nobis nec in usu erat, nomini quoque repugnatum est. Aptissimum tamen videtur mihi, quo Cicero usus est: cavillationes vocat.
passages.english: You have asked me what sophisms are called in Latin. Many have tried to give them a name; none has stuck, evidently because, since the thing itself was not accepted among us and was not in use, the name too was resisted. Yet the most fitting seems to me the one Cicero used: he calls them *cavillationes* ["quibbles"].

passages.original: Ne putes autem primum me ex nostris non ex praescripto loqui, sed meae sententiae esse: inter Cleanthen et discipulum eius Chrysippum non convenit, quid sit ambulatio. Cleanthes ait spiritum esse a principali usque in pedes permissum, Chrysippus ipsum principale. Quid est ergo, cur non ipsius Chrysippi exemplo sibi quisque se vindicet et ista tot animalia, quot mundus ipse non potest capere, derideat?
passages.english: And so that you do not think that I am the first of our school to speak not according to the rule but by my own opinion: between Cleanthes and his pupil Chrysippus there is no agreement as to what walking is. Cleanthes says it is breath sent forth from the ruling part all the way to the feet; Chrysippus, that it is the ruling part itself. Why then should not each person, following the example of Chrysippus himself, claim his freedom and laugh at all these animals, more than the world itself can hold?
passages.notes: The "ruling part" renders *principale* (Greek *hēgemonikon*). The passage is excerpted; the "animals" refers to the Stoic doctrine that virtues and the like are living beings.

passages.original: Sic Sallustio vigente anputatae sententiae et verba ante exspectatum cadentia et obscura brevitas fuere pro cultu. L. Arruntius, vir rarae frugalitatis, qui historias belli Punici scripsit, fuit Sallustianus et in illud genus nitens. Est apud Sallustium: exercitum argenta fecitt, id est, pecunia paravit. Hoc Arruntius amare coepit; posuit illud omnibus paginis. Dicit quodam loco: fugam nostris fecere. Alio loco: Hiero, rex Syracusanorum, bellum fecit.
passages.english: Thus, when Sallust was in vogue, clipped sentences, words falling before they were expected, and obscure brevity passed for elegance. Lucius Arruntius, a man of rare frugality, who wrote histories of the Punic War, was a Sallustian and strove after that style. There is in Sallust: "he made an army with silver," that is, he raised it with money. Arruntius began to love this; he put it on every page. He says in one place: "they made flight for our men." In another place: "Hiero, king of the Syracusans, made war."
passages.notes: "fecitt" taken as a scanning error for "fecit".

passages.original: Gustum tibi dare volui; totus his contexitur liber. Quae apud Sallustium rara fuerunt, apud hunc crebra sunt et paene continua, nec sine causa; ille enim in haec incidebat, at hic illa quaerebat. Vides autem, quid sequatur, ubi alicui vitium pro exemplo est.
passages.english: I wanted to give you a taste; the whole book is woven of these things. What was rare in Sallust is frequent in him and almost continuous, and not without reason: for Sallust fell upon these things, but this man went looking for them. You see, then, what follows when a fault serves someone as a model.

passages.original: Dixit Sallustius: aquis hiemantibus. Arruntius in primo libro belli Punici ait: repente hiemavit tempestas. Et alio loco cum dicere vellet frigidum annum fuisse, ait: totus hiemavit annus. Et alio loco: inde sexaginta onerarias leves praeter militem et necessarios nautarum hiemante aquilone misit.
passages.english: Sallust said: "with the waters wintering." Arruntius in the first book of the Punic War says: "suddenly the storm wintered." And in another place, when he wanted to say that the year had been cold, he says: "the whole year wintered." And in another place: "from there he sent sixty light cargo ships, besides the soldiers and the necessary sailors, with the north wind wintering."
passages.notes: "wintering" renders the verb *hiemare*, used in the sense of "to be stormy/wintry".

passages.original: Homines isti tales sunt, qualem hunc describit Horatius Flaccus, numquam eundem, ne similem quidem sibi; adeo in diversum aberrat. Multos dixi? Prope est, ut omnes sint. Nemo non cotidie et consilium mutat et votum. Modo uxorem vult habere, modo amicam, modo regnare vult, modo id agit, ne quis sit officiosior servus, modo dilatat se usque ad invidiam, modo subsidit et contrahitur infra humilitatem vere iacentium, nunc pecuniam spargit, nunc rapit.
passages.english: These men are such as Horatius Flaccus describes this one: never the same, not even like himself; so far does he stray in opposite directions. Did I say many? It is nearly all. There is no one who does not change both his plan and his wish every day. Now he wants to have a wife, now a mistress; now he wants to be king, now he takes care that no slave be more dutiful; now he puffs himself up to the point of envy, now he sinks down and shrinks below the lowliness of those who truly lie low; now he scatters money, now he seizes it.

passages.original: Qualis illorum condicio dicitur, quos natura, ut ait vergilius, sedibus nostris subditos e contrario posuit, Nosque ubi primus equis Oriens adflavit anhelis,Illis sera rubens accendit lumina Vesper; talis horum contraria omnibus non regio, sed vita est. Sunt quidam in eadem urbe antipodes, qui, ut M. Cato ait, nec orientem umquam solem viderunt nec occidentem.
passages.english:
Just as is said to be the condition of those whom nature, as Virgil says, has placed opposite, beneath our dwellings:
And when for us the rising Dawn first breathes with panting horses,
for them the reddening Evening Star kindles its late lights,
such is the life, not the region, of these people, contrary to everyone. There are certain antipodes in the same city, who, as Marcus Cato says, have never seen the sun either rising or setting.
